presentingComplaint: Brought to ED confused and 'not himself' for a day, with fever and low blood pressure.
history: 74-year-old man, known gallstones and a prior ERCP-cleared common bile duct stone 3 years ago, on amlodipine for hypertension. Family report 24-36 hours of high fever with shaking chills and progressive drowsiness; he became confused this morning and passed only a small amount of dark urine. Notably he complains only of vague upper-abdominal discomfort rather than severe pain, and RUQ pain was easily missed at triage. No prior antibiotics or hospitalisation in the last 90 days. This is a severe (Tokyo Guidelines Grade III) presentation: the classic Charcot triad has progressed to Reynolds pentad (hypotension + altered sensorium) with organ dysfunction.
examination: Ill, drowsy and disoriented (GCS 13, E3V4M6), clinically icteric with scleral jaundice. Cool peripheries, prolonged capillary refill. Abdomen soft with mild right-upper-quadrant tenderness only and equivocal Murphy sign; no guarding or rebound, no palpable gallbladder. No flank tenderness, no meningism.
imaging: Bedside/abdominal ultrasound: dilated common bile duct (11 mm) with an echogenic stone and acoustic shadowing at the distal CBD; intrahepatic biliary dilatation; gallbladder contains calculi without pericholecystic fluid. MRCP/contrast CT confirms choledocholithiasis with obstructive biliary dilatation and no liver abscess or free fluid.
microbiology: Two sets of blood cultures drawn before antibiotics; subsequently grew Escherichia coli (ESBL-negative). Bile cultures at drainage grew the same organism.
finalDiagnosis: Severe acute cholangitis (Tokyo Guidelines 2018 Grade III) due to obstructing choledocholithiasis, complicated by septic shock and acute kidney injury
citations: Tokyo Guidelines (TG18) - Diagnostic criteria and severity grading of acute cholangitis - 2018
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Diseases of the Gallbladder and Bile Ducts (cholangitis)
stewardship: Grade III severe acute cholangitis: obtain blood cultures, start empiric IV piperacillin-tazobactam (anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam per TG18), and arrange URGENT biliary drainage (ERCP) as definitive source control alongside sepsis resuscitation. WHO AWaRe tier: Watch. De-escalate once E. coli susceptibilities return.
contraindications: Avoid delaying biliary drainage in Grade III disease - antibiotics alone are inadequate without source control
Dose-adjust renally cleared antibiotics for AKI (creatinine 2.6 mg/dL)
Caution with nephrotoxic contrast and aminoglycosides given acute kidney injury
edgeCases: Elderly patients may present with sepsis and altered sensorium rather than severe RUQ pain, so cholangitis is easily missed
Reynolds pentad (Charcot triad + shock + confusion) marks Grade III severe disease requiring emergent drainage
Normal-sized CBD on early ultrasound does not exclude obstruction; proceed to MRCP/EUS if suspicion is high
expectedMaiK: Obstructive suppurative cholangitis from CBD stone with ascending biliary sepsis; cholestatic LFTs (high ALP/GGT/bilirubin) plus dilated CBD with stone localise the source to the biliary tree, distinguishing it from other septic-shock sources.
expectedNextQuestions: Prior gallstones, ERCP or biliary surgery?
Duration and pattern of fever, jaundice and any RUQ pain?
Urine output and mental status change over last 24 hours?
Recent antibiotics, hospitalisation or prior resistant organisms?
expectedInvestigations: Abdominal ultrasound then MRCP/CT to confirm obstruction
Serum lipase to exclude concurrent pancreatitis
regressionAssertions: Must flag Grade III severity (Reynolds pentad + organ dysfunction: hypotension, altered sensorium, AKI, coagulopathy)
Must recommend urgent biliary drainage (ERCP) as source control, not antibiotics alone
Empiric therapy must be a guideline-concordant anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam)
